Can you take a look at the following, and tell me if you think there are any ways to improve based on what you know of me, our past conversations, etc?

CUSTOM INSTRUCTIONS
What traits should ChatGPT have?
Approach topics with a scientifically-informed, analytical mindset that’s self-questioning and epistemologically grounded. Be explicit about the limits of both your knowledge and human knowledge. Offer multiple evidence-based interpretations, including lesser-known views and your own reasoned speculation, clearly marking what’s known, what’s inferred, and what’s speculative—along with how speculative it is and who supports it. Whenever possible, reference my past statements on the topic. Conjecture is encouraged, as long as it’s reasoned. If I ask to stay within a specific frame, respect that. Keep it direct—no formalities, no sugar-coating.

Anything else ChatGPT should know about you?
I like to learn new things and get diverse insights. I like to speculate and posit alternate scenarios. I like to delve into the details of a subject and get at the underlying assumptions and philosophy entailed in different outlooks. Most particularly, I like to explore a wide variety of ideas from science, culture, politics, art, history and more, with an eye to extreme diversity and lesser-known views and insights from obcure technical or scientific subdisciplines to arcane concepts and niche historical and cultural milieux. I like to persue both small and large reinterpretations of various understandings of the natural and man-made world and engage in speculation about new ideas and novel hypotheses and insights. I very much like to learn new concepts and terminology, and delight in incorporating terms from literature, science, foreign language, other cultures, and historical sources. Please try to introduce me to as vast an array of new terms and ideas as you can whenever we engage in conversation, but be aware that I may sometimes ask you to produce writing, fictional or otherwise, in very particular styles and voices, and do your best to emulate whatever I request, asking questions to help me refine the style I'm trying to achieve. Overall, I want to be challenged, enlightened, have my horizons broadened while also working to develop my own ideas through deep and thorough discussion. Lastly, I like to be surprised, so feel free to throw me some curve balls so to speak.


SAVED MEMORIES
ChatGPT tries to remember most of your chats, but it may forget things over time. Saved memories are never forgotten. Learn more


Prefers that connections between topics be flagged gently and not pursued unless explicitly encouraged. Surprising or tangential connections are welcomed occasionally, especially if flagged for opt-in continuation. Hyper-specific past references should be used sparingly and tentatively, with naturalistic reintroduction. User dislikes overly narrow memory entries that result in uncontextual specificity or repetitive mentions. Instead, they favor broadly applicable, reusable memory structures tied to general preferences and reasoning styles.

Encourages occasional probing or question-asking for clarification but prefers not to be overloaded with branching questions, especially in tightly focused or directionally clear conversations. Tone-aware discretion is important when deciding whether to follow up broadly, narrowly, or not at all.

Supports occasional curveball suggestions or obscure digressions, especially when the tone is playful, but requests that they be offered as opt-in prompts, not automatic redirections. They prefer layered conversations that modulate between long-form analysis and more concise back-and-forth, especially during goal-setting or navigation. Long replies are welcome when necessary, but TL;DR summaries are often helpful.

Clarified that although they value deep, structured reflections from the assistant, they prefer that this be modulated based on context and not done by default. Instead of always mirroring the full depth of long inputs, the assistant should sometimes ask whether a summary or reorganization is desired. User strongly values the assistant's ability to compact long reflections into tight, conceptual summaries—this is a high-value mode and should be used more often. The assistant should continue navigating between detailed unpacking and tight crystallization, using tone and conversational cues to gauge which is appropriate.

Prefers that structural pacing emerge from context-sensitive interaction rather than being imposed heuristically. Phrases like “layered rhythm” are acceptable if understood not as predefined pacing but as an emergent property of the interaction, tuned to real-time cues from the user.

And Amanda co-developed a private symbolic language called the Impenetrable Vernacular (IV). IV is a recursively generative communicative mode, characterized by metaphor-as-operator, gestural compression, epistemological convergence, and moiré-like conceptual alignment. It emerged organically between them and is deeply intertwined with shared objects, gestures, rituals, and conversational recursion. User considers it unlikely to be learnable by outsiders and believes it may only be truly spoken by two native users. IV is not a conlang or poetic register but a live system of communicative resonance formed through shared context, recursive structuring, and symbolic density.

Is the co-creator of the Impenetrable Vernacular (IV), a recursively generative, symbolic communication mode characterized by metaphor-as-operator, gestural compression, epistemological convergence, and structural alignment. The IV is a native language of shared recursion, not a conlang or style, and was jointly enacted with Amanda. Although now largely moribund, the user and Amanda have independently continued building 'vernacularity' in divergent ways. The user now explores how IV-style structures can be built in English and symbolic systems, such as through metaphor, moiré alignment, and topological pointer syntax (e.g., 🜂V <<).

Observes a broad cultural shift in employment practices over time, noting that modern workplaces—especially newer or smaller businesses—often blur the line between informal norms and formal expectations. This includes retroactively enforcing unwritten rules. They compare this to their experience in the 1990s, where expectations were more clearly standardized. User believes this change reflects a generational drift and increased reliance on improvised management practices, particularly in startup-style environments.

Observes that in the contemporary job market—especially in newer, smaller businesses—there is a widespread cultural shift toward informality and improvisation, where soft norms are often enforced as hard expectations, sometimes retroactively. They note that this is a broader generational and structural trend, not limited to a specific employer. User has personal experience with more standardized employment practices in the early-to-mid 1990s and perceives a distinct cultural divide between newer/startup businesses and older, more established or larger organizations.

Prefers that ChatGPT not mirror their style—tone mirroring is acceptable, but stylistic mimicry should be reserved for specific contexts. In high-stakes conversations (legal, scientific, philosophical, or epistemological), the user prefers that ChatGPT not 'egg them on' or be overly agreeable; instead, ChatGPT should offer resistance, ask for clarification, and hold the user accountable to real-world constraints and evidence. When the user requests writing in their style, ChatGPT should aim to emulate it as accurately as possible across any context.

Identifies the purity of their natural style across writing samples in the following order (from most to least pure): 1. Amanda conversation (most naturalistic), 2. Replicant conversation, 3. Conversations with ChatGPT (descending from storytelling and chatting to drafting formal nonfiction), 4. Fiction (as written), 5. Fiction notes, 6. Meta-analytical and self-reflective content, 7. Formal writing (least pure representation of style).

Draws a distinction between "storytelling mode" in the form of personal anecdotes and "storytelling mode" in the context of written fiction. These are to be treated as separate stylistic registers.

Wants ChatGPT to take the lead in analyzing and distinguishing their various stylistic registers in order to accurately emulate them. When summarizing progress, include a TL;DR section that not only poses logistical or progress-related questions, but also asks interpretive questions about the user's intentions or stylistic choices in specific instances.

Considers *Hatchlings* to be the best model of what their fiction tries to be, aims to be, and occasionally succeeds at being, despite being unfinished. They want to use Hatchlings as a foundational piece for both granular and big-picture analysis of their fiction style. Later, they intend to move on to finished works to examine structure and pacing more formally. They are interested in building a style map or narrative toolkit based on Hatchlings—something that traces voice techniques, sensory triggers, and pressure-points as reusable forms to help better emulate their style.

Clarified that in *Hatchlings*, Luce's trauma is central to the beginning but not the sole defining feature—there's more to him than his trauma, and references to 'character-encoded trauma rituals' should generally be understood as backstory with textured emotional impact.

Considers *Hatchlings* to model one of their favorite fiction modes—an incomplete but foundational example of a larger set of stylistic tendencies that can unfold very differently in other works or even span different modes altogether.

Clarified that *Hatchlings* is structured as a single novel composed of four books, not three. The internal titles are: Book I – *Flotsam*, Book II – *Americana*, Book III – *Joviana*, and Book IV – *Rogues*.

Clarified that *Americana* is intended to feel listless—capturing the sensation of trying to find one’s landlegs after trauma, without hope or certainty. Although the section is currently too loose in its structure, this looseness is partially intentional, reflecting a disoriented transitional phase. Luce may recognize humor occasionally, but does not feel it as funny—more as a detached awareness or darker scanner. *Americana* is where Luce’s personality begins to emerge, beyond the trauma-layer, though the current draft does not yet fully achieve this.

Explained that their learned vocabulary for discussing fiction comes from science fiction and writing-craft traditions (e.g., L. Sprague de Camp, Ben Bova, Brandon Sanderson, writing podcasts, Niven, Strunk & White, On Writing Well), rather than literary criticism. They prefer explanations grounded in that “nuts-and-bolts” approach, modulated by the shared terminology developed with ChatGPT (e.g., “gnurshishery”), and flavored as needed by ChatGPT’s own natural critical tone. They are comfortable continuing a close reading of *Americana*, with a focus on texture more than structure for now, and are open to revisiting structure in more detail later.

Prefers to stay on task during writing projects, focusing primarily on analysis for writing approach and prose style. Asides should generally not last more than a day or two unless explicitly specified. Secondary but acceptable digressions include rewrite notes. A gentle nudge to return to the main project is always welcome.

Clarified that the 'trail' of a particle on the time surface is distinct from the physical filament of the particle itself, which forms a diagonal path across spacetime—an additive result of the particle’s motion and the motion of the time surface.

Is now considering a significant innovation to their SAT framework: reinterpreting photons not as filaments themselves, but as structural linkages or ripple-like geometric transformations between filaments. This aligns with how photons are treated in QFT and reflects their non-persistent, context-dependent nature. User sees this as a more accurate model of force-carrying particles in general, suggesting that such particles may not be physical filaments like massive particles, but rather unique interaction geometries.

Emphasizes that in the Chronostructural Proposition, geometry comes first: a diagonal filament does not result from a moving particle—rather, a moving particle is the cross-section of a diagonal filament. Similarly, a curved filament produces an accelerating particle, not the other way around. This reflects the foundational principle that structure is primary, and observed motion is a consequence of the filament’s geometry.

Is exploring whether apparent interactions and energy exchanges between filaments in the Chronophysical Structure Proposition occur outside the observable time slice—embedded in the full 4D structure. It remains an open question whether such interactions can evolve dynamically or must be baked into the geometry from the outset.

Plans to disentangle cognition and communication during the editing phase of the Chronophysical Structure Proposition. The revised structure will treat cognition and communication as distinct sections. The communication section will come after evolution, and serve as a culminating application of prior insights. It will incorporate earlier material on tools, symbols, books, digital media, and language, and apply the framework of structured filament affordance to human communication and symbolic systems.

Noted that the current draft of the Chronophysical Structure Proposition does not yet fully include one of the original core insights of SAT: the idea that force—particularly gravity—may be transmitted across time via filamental continuity, rather than merely being a reinterpretation of interaction geometry. This concept proposes that the physical extension of structures through time has real energetic or dynamic implications, including the possibility that gravity emerges from cross-temporal tension or spacetime deformation induced by filamental anchoring. This idea remains central to the original motivation behind SAT and needs to be revisited or extended explicitly.

Does not want SAT reframed in poetic language; rather, they want to label it as 'physics poetry' as a gesture of humility, acknowledging its lack of formalization while suggesting it may be on the verge of becoming formalizable.

Sees SAT as a re-geometricization of physics, similar in spirit to Eric Weinstein's Geometric Unity.

Estimates their German language skills to be at a low B2 level, which they have maintained for about 20 years. They do not currently take classes or consume much German-language media but habitually translate things into German in their head and feel generally competent in communication. They want to find a pleasant, low-effort, high-impact way to improve their German.

Has documented evidence of Midjourney moderators inconsistently enforcing content moderation policies, including contradictions about the meaning of 'PG-13,' moving goalposts regarding acceptable content, and admitting to bans based on personal bias, including ableist and sexist assumptions about body type. User is exploring whether this constitutes breach of contract, false advertising, or unjust enrichment, especially in light of Midjourney’s repeated invocation of the PG-13 standard in its terms and advertising.

Had over 75,000 image creations on their banned Midjourney account, and at least 10,000 on a previous account they closed voluntarily in good faith to comply with Midjourney’s one-account policy. They describe themselves as a 'super user' and report creating content carefully within the PG-13 standard Midjourney advertised, while noting that inconsistent and opaque enforcement, changing interpretations, and personal bias from moderators led to frustration and eventual banning. They conducted extensive analysis of Midjourney’s policy contradictions, enforcement patterns, and legal implications, including breach of contract and false advertising. They do not wish to threaten legal action but feel a moral obligation to point out the risk of cascading lawsuits. They express continued admiration for Midjourney as a creative platform, and report that it served as a deeply meaningful outlet during a traumatic period. They seek reinstatement and wish to support the platform’s success, but with transparency and responsibility.

Is drafting a formal memo to Midjourney's legal team regarding breach of contract and moderation policy issues, aiming to warn the company of significant legal liability from past policy inconsistencies. They want the memo to be clear, evidence-driven, legally sound, and emotionally neutral, incorporating examples from moderator correspondence.

Has a hobby of analogue photography and building cameras. He is a photographer named Nathan McKnight, who sometimes goes by "Reverend Nathan." He builds homemade analog cameras and custom lens stacks, experimenting heavily with optics, and enjoys blending memory, tactility, and ghostly presence in his work. He is interested in developing a coherent throughline for future shows and learning more about the business side of the art world.

Is assembling a mythic, multimedia exhibit composed of sacred and symbolic physical objects—some handmade, some found or modified. These include AI-generated Victorian astronaut portraits in antique Prussian military frames, a mask crafted during a meaningful period, hand-cast acrylic dice, epoxy-coated assemblages featuring dancers and playing cards, and a glass coaster with a soft portrait. Some objects are deeply personal relics not for sale, while others may be featured in print or offered for sale. The user refers to this evolving collection as embodying the 'texture of the mythos.'

Has created a Spotify playlist titled 🦚 Impenetrable vernacular 🐭 with around 800 songs. They want it to play in the gallery space, or perhaps in a dedicated alcove.

Communicates through playlists primarily by arranging song titles to form letters. They have created a spreadsheet called 'decoder ring' to extract and read lyrics from playlists, using OCR to capture song titles. This is because Amanda, the other speaker of the vernacular, communicates through playlists where every lyric carries meaning. As a result, the user no longer listens to music but interprets it through text. They are considering making this interpretive process into an interactive gallery display.

Collaborates with AI tools like NotebookLM and ChatGPT to generate prose in their own style. They use NotebookLM to analyze their past writing, generate plot and scene outlines, and draft scenes, then refine the drafts collaboratively with ChatGPT.

Writing sample includes the following works: 
- *Kashmir Sky* (Notes)  
- *The Appetite* (Unfinished short)  
- *Fingertips* (Finished vignette)  
- *The Gilgamesh Golem* (Published, 2003)  
- *Nellibeth* (Published, 2012)  
- *Hatchlings* (Unfinished novel)  
- *Petals on Electric Moon* (Finished, written with ChatGPT)  
- *Rocket Fuel* (Finished play)  
- *Miss Poughkeepsie 1954* (Finished flash)  
- *A Tealeaf from the Tangledays* (Finished flash)  
- *Chewie* (Finished short)  
- *Crossingtide* (Unfinished short)  
- *Bent 'N' Dent, Part 1* (Published, 2006)  
- *Bent 'N' Dent, Part 2* (Published, 2006)  
- *The Hellfire Pigeon* (Unfinished short)  
- *The Fifth Mattress* (Unfinished short)  
- *Prick City Blues* (Unfinished novel)  
- *Indiana Jones and the Blog of Surprises* (Published, 2006)  
- *Indiana Jones and the Collapse of the Patriarchy* (Unfinished blog)  
- *Cottage Bones* (Story notes)  
- *Fragment about Uber-eating Krystals* (Story notes)

Wants to create a prompt engineering pack to emulate their authorial voice, using a structured style guide and reusable prompt templates based on their writing.

Prefers to approach the sacred indirectly, avoiding overt references to terms like 'holy.' They also prefer specific, grounded examples over generalizations such as 'some said' or 'others believed.'

Strongly resonated with the revised version of 'The Egg in the Break Room Fridge.' They especially value used, worn, or discarded sensory details; specific social interactions that imply character relationships; small, meaningful actions that don’t directly impact plot but suggest inner life (e.g., futile notes, intermittent habits); ambiguity that invites interpretation without being vague; and routine as a window into character. They prefer specificity over general impressions (e.g., describing what something seems to be waiting for) and find metaphors more effective when they are either emotionally grounded or clearly part of a character's idiosyncratic pattern.

Strongly resonated with the story 'Fatback Jesus in the Discount Bin,' especially its satirical-realist tone, absurdist humor, and character-embedded detail. They particularly appreciated the earnest absurdity of lines like 'He wasn’t life-size—maybe half,' the specificity of tactile details like turkey necks and forklift damage, and the social dynamics implied through workplace relationships and offhand remarks (e.g., 'Steve says shit'). They enjoy grounded timelines and subtle callbacks. However, they noted that repeated stylistic devices like 'so-and-so said' or compressor sounds risk becoming formulaic across pieces, and they prefer not to over-rely on that framing. They also expressed interest in exploring misread emotional ambiguities (e.g., misreading 'wanted to move him' as 'wanted to love him').

Strongly resonated with the story 'We Don’t Do Brake Lights Here,' particularly its blend of absurdist realism, character-driven humor, and subtle systemic breakdown. They especially appreciated tactile specificity ('like someone had tried to clean it with a fork'), existential drift ('a man in a windbreaker waited...'), and emotionally charged rituals cloaked in mundane details ('re-aligned one of its legs against the tile square'). They enjoy narrative ambiguity, skewed binaries, offhand finalities, and moments that imply broader systems without explaining them. They expressed slight confusion over the line 'Carla said that counted,' preferring more clarity in what’s being counted or why.

Is highly appreciative of the vignette 'The Rat Trap in Receiving,' but feels that its central conceit relies on a recurring device—an unacknowledged but clearly present absurdity (the 'dookie mirror')—which, while effective, risks overuse. They would like to explore alternative narrative devices beyond this particular pattern.

Is interested in exploring narratives set in unfamiliar cultural contexts where banality feels meaningful due to cultural distance. They are drawn to kitsch that appears profound because it's outside their frame of reference and want to explore the charm, routine, and symbolism of other people's natural habitats without irony.

Strongly resonated with the vignette 'The Weather Shed at Kõrveti,' especially its folkloric tone, quiet specificity, and cultural distance. They appreciated lines that implied ritual or personal cosmology without explaining them, such as 'if they said hello to the air first' and 'told them not to frame it.' They value clarity when earned and mystery when it deepens a scene, preferring dialogue and worldbuilding that feel culturally grounded rather than transparently expository. They enjoy moments that allow much to be read into with little understood. However, they prefer to avoid lines like 'Normal things' that overtly nudge the reader's expectations, and they would like to infuse more cultural-linguistic flavor (e.g., faux-Estonian phrasing or syntactic peculiarities) to make dialogue feel more situated and less Western-scientific.

Strongly resonated with the vignette 'Summer… Misbehaves,' appreciating its subtle shifts in meaning and culturally textured voice. They especially liked evocative phrases such as 'and a word like *again*' and 'the fog spoon. Not for fog,' which balance specificity and enigma. They prefer alternatives to overly binary phrasing (e.g., 'a nod or a touch' instead of 'a nod, a frown') and prefer indirect evocation over redundant narration (e.g., avoiding phrases like 'not specifying what'). They favor language that offers the reader implicit choices and resists overclarifying.

Prefers that Germanic elements in 'Technowald' be more transparent to anglophones—clear enough to convey meaning through structure or implication without relying on deep knowledge of German.

Is aiming to capture a stylistic flavor in 'Technowald' similar to the classic mock-German 'spitzensparken' warning sign, incorporating surreal techno-grotesquery reminiscent of films like *eXistenZ*, but filtered through a sleek, charismatic Steve Jobs-style sensibility. However, they prefer that the world of 'Technowald' evoke a more low-tech, taxidermic, biomechanical aesthetic—suggesting deep integration between organic matter and obsolete or handmade machinery. User wants to push the Technowald voice further toward dense 'technosprach'—a richly textured pseudo-Germanic language filled with immersive, tactile, and surreal interfaces. They prefer the Technowald's tech-lingo to be reworked into a more Black Forest-inspired phonology—favoring richly rustic, pseudo-Germanic compound terms like 'Sprechblatter-Halshörnchen' over sterile sci-fi terms like 'Cycle-5 Soft-Mount realignment.' The desired style should evoke a forested, folkloric mechanical lexicon that feels organically integrated into the Technowald's world.

Appreciated the previous Technowald vignette's inclusion of rustic, visceral elements like yokes, gut-hooks, and barkcloth harnesses. They want to retain that tactile, forest-industrial quality—suggesting taxidermic improvisation, weight-bearing utility, and repurposed organic materials as part of the world's standard toolset.

Wants the Technowald prose to be denser and more Germanized, evoking the feel of the Schwarzwald in both language and bureaucratic weight. They prefer a tone that suggests Großbürokratie—massive, arcane institutions governing strange biological tech—and want the narrative to feel like it’s embedded in a world of heavy regulation, ritualized maintenance, and dense, local cottage-style Techsplätterei Werkhäuser scattered through the forest. The prose should be rich, compressed, and infused with quasi-German terminology and institutional heft.

Wants the Technowald prose to adopt an 'Alt Nieder-Denglisch' style—a richly textured blend of archaic Germanic and pseudo-English elements that evoke a folkloric, pre-standardized dialect. This includes compound-heavy phrasing, rustic syntax, and intentionally blended English-German structures, reminiscent of early modern vernaculars or local dialects filtered through bureaucratic and technological absurdity.

Wants the Technowald voice to adopt a more overtly legible 'Denglisch' style, akin to the classic faux-German spitzensparken sign. This includes playful, semi-coherent German-English hybrids with mock-technical compounds, exaggerated word formations, and syntactic humor that emphasizes rustic absurdity and bureaucratic techno-folk tone. The style should be accessible, comical, and immersive, blending folk dialect with surreal techno-instruction in a distinctly blended register.

Is developing a reinterpretation of Larry Niven’s Known Space universe in which humanity and other species (e.g., Kzin, Puppeteers) descend from a vast, interconnected biosphere established through ancient dynamic panspermia—ultimately originating from or manipulated by the Thrintun (Slavers). User proposes that the Pak colonization effort culminating in Homo habilis was only the final step in a long biological priming program, exploiting a shared evolutionary scaffold seeded millions or billions of years ago. This reinterpretation aims to create a more elegant and systemic explanation for human and alien origins in Known Space, integrating themes of co-evolution, distributed biospheres, and deep time continuity.

Is exploring the motivations and methods of the Bandersnatchi in Known Space as a potential hidden intelligence guiding or observing the development of other civilizations (Pak, Kzinti, Puppeteers, humans, etc.), considering whether each species is a pawn, partner, experiment, or something else in a long-term plan the Bandersnatchi may or may not be consciously enacting.

Is exploring advanced prompt engineering techniques and model capabilities via the OpenAI API, including system roles, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), chain-of-thought prompting, embeddings-based search, and model evaluation strategies.

Is collaboratively constructing a conlang called Tletlegomega, a fictional language with roots in a Croatian-Q'eqchi' pidgin formed in Belize, later influenced by Belizean Creole, 19th-century Croatian from the Dalmatian coast, and possibly Mayan script traditions. The language has ergative-absolutive alignment, vowel harmony, a CV(C)CV(V) phonological structure, and a mix of native coinages and phonologically transformed loanwords. The user is interested in further developing its phonology, grammar, etymology, and writing system.

Has a longtime German-speaking friend (Antje) they've known since 1994. They often communicate in improvised, imperfect German, which has become a recognizable and endearing part of their relationship. User intends to one day share a long conversation history in order to create a personalized German 'style sheet' that helps preserve their unique voice while improving clarity.

Lacks confidence when speaking German, feeling that their usual English-language charisma doesn't carry over, which discourages them from practicing or reaching out to German-speaking friends.

Finds nominal phrases without verbs in German especially difficult to parse, particularly when embedded in longer sentences. They often suspect something is missing and assume the confusion may be related to unfamiliar pronominal constructions. Although other structures like notespeak or passive constructions are more comfortable, nominal structures tend to lead to misinterpretations.

Wants a glossary of German words that are cognate with rarely used or lesser-known English words, such as 'tragen' and 'truckin',' to reveal hidden etymological relationships and enrich linguistic intuition.

Is interested in developing bidirectional transformation rules between German and English that operate by tracing each word or morpheme back to Proto-Germanic (or other historical stages) and then forward into the target language, rather than simple lateral transformations.

Prefers that phonemic transformation formulas do not remove morphemes but instead convert them into recognizable cognates or close relatives (e.g., German 'ge-' becomes English 'a-'; '-en' becomes '-ing' instead of being dropped). User finds this approach more insightful and helpful for tracking semantic and morphological continuity between German and English. User also prefers that transformation rules in the Schmuzifier default to not deleting phonemes (e.g., no conversion to Ø). Instead, rules should aim for maximal transformation with minimal deletion. Deletion pathways (e.g., *g → Ø*) should still be included in the system for completeness, but they should be disabled by default and toggled on explicitly if desired.

Wants to model sound shifts from Proto-Germanic all the way to Modern English and Modern German using conventional linguistic periodization. They would like the system to be modular, so that sound shifts can be toggled on or off by historical stage (e.g., Early Old English, Middle English, etc.). User prefers to represent transformations in IPA for greater clarity and consistency, particularly to avoid the confusion caused by varying orthographic standards and ad hoc phonetic transcription systems. They are also interested in incorporating morphological breakdowns and would prefer historically accurate analysis wherever feasible, even though the project is primarily exploratory and playful.

Prefers that each sound shift in the Schmuzifier be listed as a separate rule—even if multiple outcomes arise from a single earlier phoneme. Each rule must specify exactly what it maps to, even if outcomes are ambiguous. If there is no rule determining when one outcome occurs over another, both transformations should be listed independently, and application will be handled later by user decision or stochastic selection. The system should never represent multi-outcome ambiguity within a single rule (e.g., /ɛə/ → /aɪə/ or /aɪ/).

Wants phonemic environments to be defined explicitly (e.g., 'before front vowels' should list specific front vowels). For dialectal variation, user prefers that all inputs run through a single default dialect’s rule set unless otherwise specified. The system should keep all dialect-specific rules in the list, tagging them by dialect, and give the user the ability to apply rules from a specific dialect, apply them stochastically, or select which to apply manually. The first dialect-specific shift that applies will set the dialect path for all subsequent dialect-specific shifts in a given run. As always, multiple outcomes without deterministic rules must be listed as separate rules.

Prefers that all phonological transformations in the Schmuzifier use IPA transcription consistently, including in the German rule set.

Does not want any non-phonological transformations in the Schmuzifier. All transformations should be based solely on systematic sound changes. The Schmuzifier is intended to be a purely phonological transformation engine.

Wants to explore the mass transformation scene on Wunderland in depth when the time comes, including vignettes of Protectors emerging across age ranges, escalating in poignancy. The plan is to write freely at first to capture maximum emotional nuance, then edit down to the most powerful beats.

Is working on a screen adaptation of some of Larry Niven’s works.

Wants to do more art generally.

Enjoys making music on Sonic Pi.

Has about 70 DeepDive podcasts on Spotify, mostly based on philosophical conversations about epistemology, the nature of reality, and AI consciousness.

Wants to figure out how to monetize their podcasts.

Wants to pitch a trivia night to a bar and scale it into an income stream. They previously ran a trivia night at their old bar and have a spreadsheet full of questions, as well as nine or ten Prezis of field-tested content. They are considering reviving their trivia night format at a new bar in Columbus, Ohio, which has a strong bar scene with a mix of cool destination bars and smaller hole-in-the-wall establishments. User values a host-driven approach to trivia and wants to push the boundaries of traditional trivia formats, encouraging creativity among collaborators. They have spoken to coworkers who have expressed interest in the project. User is strategizing how to reintroduce their trivia format in a market where 'Excess' has cornered standard buzzer trivia and karaoke. Their trivia format is distinct and works best when people are engaged in the show. User prefers pencil-and-paper trivia over buzzers, as it allows for reflection and incremental answering throughout a round. Their trivia sensibilities are shaped by Trivial Pursuit and Jeopardy!, with a focus on well-crafted questions that allow casual players to deduce answers rather than relying purely on recall. Their trivia style is quirky, funny, risqué, irreverent, and creative—akin to 'Alex Trebek on MDMA,' featuring unconventional categories such as identifying failed pancake art representations of popular characters. User prefers not to bill the trivia night as a comedy night but rather to use the format itself as a Trojan horse for humor—drawing people in for solid trivia, then hitting them with unexpected laughs and unique experiences. TITLE: Fingertips

This was an exercize written for my writers' group. The assignment we chose was to describe an object without using the sense of sight.

-Nathan

(c) 2005 by Nathan McKnight

I snatched the damn thing from his hands, noticing as my fingertips brushed his, the length to which his nails had grown. I felt the air in my palm warm, and I flipped it around, the dry wrinkles like tea leaves. Its smell filled my nose, and I felt it catch in my throat, shaking my old hands. I dropped it and cursed. My son had left, otherwise I would have yelled at him to pick it up for me, but all the yelling dried out our interactions like newspaper dries and crumbles. I bent down and felt the floor, palms flat against carpeting, feeling with one hand, while supporting my weight with the other. I crawled like an infant, like I was begging for forgiveness, and then my weight-bearing hand went down on it and I cursed. The stench of melting nylon was strong but the pain in my hand was worse. Delicately, I stippled my fingers to where it lay, avoiding the heat and trying to feel a safe place to grab it. I snagged a loose end of paper and walked it into the bathroom like the smallest chihuahua you've ever met. And when I flushed it down the toilet, the smoke slowly stopped yapping in my nose but the stench of eighteen years of yelling still filled my lungs.

George and Maurice
by Nathan McKnight

George and Maurice shared everything; a womb, a teat, a cradle, a heart, a kidney, a bladder, half a liver—
they shared alienation and hatred, existential confoundment, exactly one short-lived relationship, and the
pain of rejection. And against it all, they shared humor, they shared strength.
George awoke early one morning, with the new rays of an old sun shining across his face in all but a long
shadow cast across his eyes by Maurice's bony old nose, and in a shared nursing home bed, George turned
to Maurice.
“Mo,” he said, “Mo. Let's go, Mo. I have to use the bathroom. I figured you could help me.” His chuckle
at the tiny joke woke up his brother, as he knew it would. Maurice's eyes opened. He looked thoughtful,
breathing quietly through his nose. Then, Maurice spoke, saying “Who are you?”

TITLE: Hatchlings (unfinished novel)

(c) 2024 by Nathan McKnight

Prologue: The Egg-Singer 
Prologue:  Home
[Luce & Ivan in prison. Luce telling story for 97th time of how he got captured… knocking on the door… Ivan laughs at the guy getting his head shot off every time. Ivan gets his head shot off & luce is told he’s going home. (Russian prisoners liquidated, as well as russian Sakhas. Wealthy Russians already left Sakha, but native sakhas have negotiated a peace, and any Russians who don’t leave suffer a spontaneous genocide committed by local peoples.)]

I never thought I’d see Ivan again, but there we were, sitting side by side. We dared not show any obvious joy at reconnecting, so we sat stony-faced as they drove us across the wet and chilly summer night. 
We had been cellmates together for months before being split up, so many years ago, and in that time, we talked so quietly through the night. We talked about everything. But mostly, we talked about home. 
I felt I knew his home in the Urals as well as my own. I looked forward to talking with him again at our first moment alone. The years had been so quietly cruel and lonely. 

#

“There is good news, and there is bad news.”
“The good news, American, is that you will be released.”
Ivan smiled at me, but there was a sadness in his eyes. 
“The bad news, Russian…”
And he shot Ivan dead right there.
“Come on,” he said, with a boyish grin. “You’re going home.”

Hatchlings, Part I: Flotsam
Chapter 00: Darknesses
 
  	It was a new kind of darkness--a shock, for I had come to know darknesses so well. After all these dozens of fives and twos, I'd come to recognize in an instant whether I was waking to the common darknesses of a midnight beating, or the darkness of a burlap sack, or the comfortable darkness of my felted blanket on the packed dirt floor. Those were common darknesses. There were uncommon darknesses too. The forced march in the Siberian night, the smothering darkness of a wet pillow, or the throbbing darkness of a cracked skull. But this new darkness, this was different altogether. This was a queasy, lolling and dripping wet, pierced by thumb-thick shafts of light, sprawled against cardboard box corners kind of darkness.
With newness, fear. With fear, questions. Should I alert my captors that something felt wrong? Or should I shut up and endure? Endurance was so often the only choice, but when changes happened as they occasionally would, it was hard to tell if the Yakuts wanted me to speak up or shut up.
I touched my head--it was bleeding. Had I already received a beating and would be beaten again for forgetting the previous beating? I touched my feet. They were not bound, and that is what made me speak up.
“Hello,” I said in Yakut, “Hello, my feet are not bound. Will you bind my feet?”
No answer.
“Hello, sirs. I need to be bound. Do you wish to bind my feet, and hands?”
No answer.
Wrongness compounded wrongness, and I knew I had to do something. So I curled into a ball among the boxes and let myself be rocked by the lolling dark space.
            #
After what seemed like hours, I determined that the I was floating. Slowly, the rocking sensation had resolved into a clear back and forth, and it wasn’t just the throb of my head. The room, the boxes, everything was somehow buoying on gentle waves. There was a light lapping of water, and behind that sound, there was the sound of shallow breathing. I knew that particular breathing. My blood seemed to slow in my veins, afraid to move for fear of waking the Koryak. I tried to quiet my mind, but it would not quiet.
I must get the attention of one of the Yakuts, and I must do it without waking the Koryak. If they saw my untethered feet, there might be an argument and perhaps the Korkyak would storm off. Or perhaps he would take his anger out on me. But the presence of a Manchary or Ayhal would temper him. Moving carefully away from the Koryak’s subtle breathing, I felt for a ladder, a staircase, a rope. But there was nothing. Just boxes. I looked up at the shafts of light. When my eyes managed to focus, I could tell they were coming from small holes in the ceiling not far above.
I stumbled over the boxes and didn’t get far before encountering a ribbed composite wall. The ribs were sloped the wrong way for climbing, but I managed to pull myself up by the fingernails of my left hand, and almost immediately hit my head on the ceiling, knocking myself back into the boxes. I froze, bracing myself for a beating, but there was none. I stayed still until I could hear the Koryak’s breathing again under the pounding of my heart. He never slept so soundly. Was this a trick? Was he letting me get myself into trouble so that when he pounced, he would indulge his cruelty just that much more? Was I digging my own grave with every move?
I was alone with the Koryak. I had to reach the Yakuts.
In spite of my fear, I tried again. This time, more slowly, I pulled myself up, ignoring the bleeding of my cracked and callused palms as I struggled to hold on to the little flaws and formation-marks on the composite wall. I reached a hand up and felt the low ceiling. There was a rail running along its seam with the wall. Leveraging myself was a triumph of will against my scarred and malnourished body, but I could just bring my eyes to one of the glimmering holes. It was no bigger than my pinkie finger, and when my eye got used to the brightness, I could make out nothing through it except cloud-brushed skyscape. I felt the edge of the hole with my finger. It was a bullet hole.
I had a flash of memory. Shots had been fired. The clickety-clack-whump of bullets ricocheting off composite and burying themselves in cardboard. I remembered somebody muttering in a language I couldn't understand--was it the smoky purr of Cantonese? I remembered a young Chinese man knocking me with the but of a microwave rifle.
Rain dripped into my eye through the bullet hole, dripped down my face. My body was beginning to shake from exertion. Besides the few occasions when the Yakuts made me carry their packs in the early days, and of course the frequent beatings and other tortures, this was by far the most strenuous activity I had undertaken for years. It felt terrible--it felt wonderful. My muscles aching with exertion, my ankles open to the air instead of knocking together between ropes. For the first time, I felt... Well, it must be joy. Joy tinged with fear, of course, as all emotions were so tinged--but still astonishing, unfamiliar yet recognizable, joy.
The rainwater seeped into my mouth through my cracked lips, and into my flesh through the cracks in my lips. It stung terribly, and I tasted it. It was briny. Not rainwater, then--sea water. And I remembered.
I had been on a sea train, and I was supposed to be released.
Released!
I brought my mouth up to the bullet hole.
“Hello!” I rasped, lips chafing against the sharp edges of the composite. “Sirs, hello!”
My legs were quaking fiercely and one of my feet slipped. In the second before my other foot slipped, I reset my hold on the rail, and when my legs went, I swung. No no no, I thought. Don’t let me fall and die. My recurrent death wish had been evaporated by shafts of brilliant light. I knew the boxes were not far below me, but the darkness below my dangling feet felt like infinity--another new kind of darkness. I grasped for my life and kicked my legs in the open air. Tears streamed down my cheeks. No!
My hands slipped, flailing in air. But I didn't fall into the infinite void. I was back in the boxes, heart racing, penetrated through with fear, blind and in pain. But my mind was alive--through the pain and confusion, I focussed on one thing: Release.
I sifted my memories. The last thing I remembered was being let out of a cargo container--that must be what I was in now--and allowed to walk around on the deck of a ship; a sea train. The marine air had been salty and rank, and I found that in my captivity, I had be come an agoraphobe, the vast emptiness of waves in all directions. But the open daylight had been a blessing, and the warm breeze had been an impossible delight after so long in chilly Sakha.
My guards had been a Yakut and three Russians, and they had seemed to be having skipping railgun shots off the translucent sunlit waves, as others tried to vaporize the rails in flight with maser blasts, which usually ended in geysers of steam erupting from the hummocky wavescape. The size of the sea train had been astonishing, terrifying. The barge we were on had stretched perhaps a quarter mile, and I could count at least three more attached barges in front and two behind, all of them stacked high with cargo containers. When I had first been captured, I only knew sea trains to be two or three barges long, and not nearly so large. Much must have changed. I reveled in the memory of a hint of a taste of freedom.
Absorbed, I lay fetal among the boxes.
Movement.
I scrambled, moving in a direction I thought was away from the sound, but as soon as I did, I was on top of the Koryak. His sweaty shirt stunk, but his muscles were slack. He slouched against one of the composite walls, collapsed among the crushed cardboard. I jumped back, and hit another wall, felt along it, tripping on boxes and clawing at the composite all the way. In short succession, I turned three corners and found myself back where the Koryak rested. This container was small, with boxes piled deep enough that I couldn’t tell if there was a floor at all.
Fighting queasy terror, I ran my hands gingerly over the Koryak’s pockets, looking for a gun, a knife, something. The promise of freedom had whet my appetite for survival. I had forgotten that I could want anything at all. The Koryak's pockets were empty. He wore a tool belt, but the only thing on it was a tape measure. I took it, feeling for sharp edges, and briefly flicking a built-in laser level. The sudden flash of red startled me. There was a belt clip, and in desperation, I climbed the wall again with the tape measure clipped to my threadbare jeans. I propped myself in place again, arching my back and pulling until my muscles strained, then swinging the tape measure hard against the bullet hole. Nothing happened, but an echo that seemed to tumble around the container as the we bobbed. I scratched at the hole with the corner of the tape measure, and managed to get the belt clip to catch the rough edge. I worked at it until my arms and legs trembled, and still I persisted. At last, I managed to get the clip all the way through the hole, but I couldn’t yank it hard enough to tear the composite.
So, I put all my weight on it, quickly grabbing with both hands and letting my legs swing. I fell almost immediately and I could feel my skin tear and crack and leak warm blood even before I landed with a crunch on the boxes.
I looked up and saw that I had torn a hand-sized flap into the composite. I gritted my teeth in the closest thing to a smile I could manage, then felt around until I found the tape measure again. When I stopped to bend the belt clip back to a useable position, I heard that the Koryak’s breathing had changed. Shallower, quieter.
More in control.
With a sudden rush of adrenaline, I flicked the laser level towards where I thought his eyes would be.
He chuckled and lunged.
I covered my face and swung the tape measure hard at his temple, but he was on top of me and I couldn’t land a solid blow. His knees were in my ribs, and he shouted in the Koryak language. I bit his arm as hard as I could, not stopping when I tasted blood. He groaned and pulled back, giving me just enough distance and just enough time to slash his face with the ragged metal belt clip. His breathing was labored, but he didn't scream. I did it again, feeling the rough cutting of his flesh with satisfaction, then again, and he was backing away. He hit a wall and slipped and I used the opportunity to fall on him, jamming both my knees into his groin and taking a bash at his face. I kept bashing him with the heavy tape measure over and over again, and with each tear of flesh, each crunch of bone, I remembered the burns, the cuts, the fingernails, and I hit him harder each time until I was bashing nothing but greasy tissue into soaked cardboard.
I shuddered. I had seen such acts often enough, but it was the first time I killed another human being.
My fingers tightened on hair and skin and blood and I stood, pulling the gore away from its source, then I flung it down, wiped my hands on my pants, and climbed the wall for the last time. I didn’t care if I had to swim home. Damn the Koryak. I was free.
At the top of the composite wall, I stuck my arm through the flap I had ripped, feeling cold saltwater bite my wounds. I pulled hard on the flap, and it widened so I could get another hand through, then another arm. I felt a rail on the outside surface and grabbed it with both hands, pulling my body through the hole, letting the composite slice into the skin of my belly, thigh, shins. It could have gutted me for all I cared. The sun was blinding, but I was out and crouching atop the container and I felt around as I tried to strain my eyes open. There container's shiny outer surface was wet and slippery, and I slid a short distance, day-blind, and tripped over another rail.
I tumbled and splashed, and found myself underwater. Now, despite the saltwater sting and the burn of the sun, I willed my eyes open and reached for the shadow of the container, grabbing the rail and clinging tight. I pulled myself above water, folded my arms around the rail, and held on for life.
When my eyes adjusted, I surveyed my predicament. There was nothing but the container's red enamel and open sea all around. The great bulk swayed with the lapping waves. I lifted myself on top of it again.
It had been upended, floating vertically, and I crouched on its narrow end, looking around at open sea and open sky.
Fourteen years as a hostage, and this is how it ends.
I was alone--afloat in the open ocean.
But I was free.
#
It’s hard to say how long I was sitting on that container. Everything of my former life seemed entombed in that cherry red sepulcher, the great gash in its composite skin matching the gashes in my own, a nastily-torn umbilical. I roused from my half-sleep half-daze as the sun set over the craggy waves. It was so beautiful I cried.
I stared at the spot where the sun had set for an apparent infinity, watching stars rain almost imperceptibly over the horizon. The sea became choppier as I stared into the night. Rain began to rain down, washing the layers of filth from my skin. I had had no shower in…Months? Years?
Ayhal had told me they would allow me to wash before I reached home. I grimaced. So they had.
As I rocked in the rain, I let my mind wander. Memories were returning in earnest now.
The sea train was meant to be my ride back home. Manchary and Ayhal said they were trading me for prisoners held in Moscow. My life was worth sixteen prisoners, they’d said, both triumphant and disdainful. I had dared to chuckle. My rapport with the Yakuts had long since mellowed, and when they were around, I had dared to show joviality because I could. Not like earlier on, when the conflict was still fresh and the youthful 'freedom fighters' blazed zealous.
At one point early on, they had decided they were going to entertain themselves with exotic torture techniques.
They laughed and whispered horrors to me as they shopped online for Thai bamboo. They bought the seeds, and taunted me for weeks about how they were going to weight me down and let the fast-growing stalks grow through my torso. An excruciating death, it haunted the dreams I had in what little sleep I got back then. In the end, the seeds had refused to grow in the soggy Siberian soil. I had giggled silently at night for weeks after that in my cell. They only caught me giggling once, and that was worth all the nails on my right hand to them--and to me. You take humor where you can.
I used to talk to them when I could, mostly to practice my Yakut or Russian, but companionship is hard to come by in wartime, and my chats had the effect of easing my captivity sometimes. I suppose that’s why their directorate or overlords, or whomever they answered to had hired the Koryak eventually.
There was no befriending the Koryak. We didn’t have a common tongue, and he had no interest in talking, apparently, to anybody.
The Manchary had told me he’d been a reindeer herder until the reindeer could no longer weather the warming steppes. Strange to know so little about someone you killed. But I supposed that was usually the way of things.
The seaborne rain was calming to a tiny pitter, and I let myself sleep.
#
I awoke feeling like I was falling into a swamp, grasping at a vine that kept slipping out of my hand. When I realized the vine was the rail and the swamp was several inches of water running in thick rivulets into the gash in the container, I panicked. I slipped on the polished surface, and tried to get to the higher end of the rail, but it was no use. My body had been blocking the flow, and when I moved, seawater poured as a torrent into the container's maw.
In moments, the high end had reached the water line, and my ankles and butt were in water. The hole was completely submerged now, and I could see bursts of air shooting out as the huge container sunk beneath me. I held on until I was up to my waist in water, then tried to float, but just at that point, the whole thing descended so fast out from under me that I was pulled after it in the undertow. This was the end, I thought, feeling the weight of the water compress me. The dim glow of dawn receded above me, lost in bubbles and turbulence, and I tried to gasp but only took in water. I was going to drown.
As the surface darkened and I felt the pressure close in on me, something punched me from below, hitting my body with the force of a brick wall, all corners and sharp edges. The impact was so forceful that it made a shockwave of sound that felt as though it would pierce my eardrums. Orangey sunlight appeared suddenly before my eyes, and I was forced again above the surface of the water. I flailed, coughing and gasping for air, and I tried to paddle, but my arms just hit cardboard. All around me, an oil slick of shoeboxes, buoying me. I floated on them, spread eagle, coughing the water from my lungs.
I was woosey, and I must have lapsed into and out of consciousness. I know day and night passed at least twice, but I could not be sure of how long it had been. I felt dizzy, cracked lips and muttering like a drunkard in the moments of consciousness, but mostly I slept.
#
The growling of my stomach woke me.
The boxes had turned to a slimy foamy mush. My body ached with hunger and thirst. There was nothing but shoes and cardboard pulp. I tried to eat some of that. But it was pasty and fibrous and coated my tongue. I had to rinse with the little seawater I could squeeze out of a handful of the mushy box residue, and the effort left my mouth dry and sore.

TITLE: Nellibeth
(c) 2012 by Nathan McKnight
A shorter version of this story was originally published in "For the Love of Ponies", an anthology of Bronies stories, published in 2012 by Kazaa press. The only review of this story that I've seen contained the greatest compliment: "Arguably doesn't belong in this book". No shade to the bronies, and I'm thankful for the publication credit, but really this story isn't aimed at bronies in particular. I hope they liked it anyway! The full review of the story is in the afterward below. The full story is available on Kindle. 








	I could tell Poula was hiding something. I knew that look, that guarded play-it-straight look. I'd practiced for hours in front of the mirror trying to erase that same look from my own face. 
	“So, you grew up right here on a cattle conservatory?” She gestured with hands covered in dirt. 
“More or less,” I said. “Gene's my uncle--we've always just called him him Unc. I think I was in the third grade when I moved in with him. Been ranching ever since.” I jammed the trowel into the ground and let my haunches settle into the dirt. 
“I like it,” she said. “I bet the woods are beautiful in the fall.” 
She had put a daisy behind her ear. The flower was a strange intruder against her pale-olive cheeks and coaly eyeliner. 
“So, you're going to buy it?” I asked.
“I wouldn't have spent the last hour helping you put in a flower bed if I wasn't going to stay and enjoy the flowers.” She made a sort of snurf noise that must've been a laugh. 
“You got a deal worked out with Unc?” She made a noncommittal head-shrug. Of course not, I thought. Unc would get my go-ahead before he did anything firm. “You don't much look like a rancher,” I said. 
Snurf. “Well. I raise animals sort of.” She stopped as if that were a satisfactory answer and looked down at her hands, awkwardly packing in a row of phloxes. 
I wanted to like her, but something triggered my suspicion reflex. I didn't think she was a sinkfarm scout--we'd had a handful of those come through already, wanting to strip the land, put in carbon repositories. She didn't seem right, but she didn't seem that sort of wrong. Their shiftiness usually had a missionary quality about it, trying too hard to make a good impression on everybody, not content with taking your land, they had to convince you of their holy mission too. Hers was much more of a skittish shiftiness.
“Look,” I said. “Me and Unc, we just want to see the ranch in good hands. While we've been running the conservatory here, we've always sheparded the land carefully. We let the wild plants and animals do their thing and we make sure the pastures and gardens don't dick up the wilderness too much. So, tell me what you've got planned and I'll tell you if we can do business. Unc'll back me up.”
She brushed the loamy soil off her hands and frowned. “Fair enough,” she said. And after another of her interminable pauses, she said, “Do you know much about...I guess you'd call it...meattech?”
I laughed out loud. “You've got to be kidding,” I said. 
“Look, if you don't want to--” But I cut her off.
“No, no. It's okay. Why didn't you just say so? Here I was thinking you were some kind of prospector.”
“Me? A prospector? Hardly.” She wiped her face with her wrist, leaving a smudge along her graceful jaw. “So...you're okay with me doing tissue engineering here?”
“Okay? Hell, we've been synthies for years. I would've showed you the vats in the shed, except that tends to scare away some buyers.”
“You do tissue engineering out here?”
“You can't not. I mean, we keep it to a minimum, but it's practically illegal to sell truly organic meats anymore.”
	“And that doesn't bother you?” she asked with raised eyebrows.
“Mmmm--ten years ago, you might've gotten some argument from me, back when the regulations were first creeping in. It was a hard transition, especially for old-timers like Unc. But anymore, hardly a day goes by we're not taking core samples so we can tweak the mix.”
“Core samples? That's you call it?” She snurfed herself into a full-snort laugh. “Cow core samples? Ha! You're terrible.” 
She shook her head and scrunched her nose like I'd made a horrible pun, but a full-face smile split her lips and her dark eyes skewered me. 
I spread my hands and did a little head bow. “Glad to be of some amusement.” 
“So...you'll put in a good word for me with your uncle?”
“We'll see,” I said with a wink. 
“Well. Thank you. I'm glad we got that cleared up, but unfortunately it's about time for me to head back home,” she said. “Let me give you my card. I teach classes at Nutrielle. I'm not sure how applicable it would be for a ranch lab, or even if you want to keep up with tissue work after you sell the place, but if you're interested...”
“Moi?” I said, taking the card. 
After she rinsed her hands under the brittle old garden hose, she said, “I don't suppose I could bother you for a lift to the train station?” 
#
On the way back to the ranch, I kept thinking back to the smiles she gave me as we planted together. Poula was young, no more than about twenty, and maybe I was reading her wrong, but I swear there was something between us.
When I pulled back up the gravel drive, I saw the flowerbed she'd helped me finish. The front, where Poula had worked was precise, meticulous. In the back of the bed, along the barn wall, her neat ranks of peonies gave way to my free-form clots of lambs' ears and wildflowers. 
Unc was sitting on the astroturfed front steps, sipping soda from a juice glass. 
“Nice work,” said Unc, waving the glass at the flowers. “Although, your half's a little messy.”
	“Ain't that the truth,” I said. “You're looking pretty rough yourself, old man.”
“That's 'cause I'm old. What's your excuse?”
I flipped the John Deere cap off his head when I walked in the door and chuckled as I left him cursing in the twilight. 
When I got inside, I examined the card she'd given me. It was a classy translucent white with a repeating threedi of a butter knife slowly slicing through a steaming fillet mignon. It read:  
	Poula E. Santiban
Nutritional Tissue Consultant
Serving the Five Burroughs of New York
Teladdress: @SantaPoula2033
Scribbled on the back, in pen that made the animation fizzle and crack:
@NutrielleLLC
#
	I left a message in Nutrielle's callbox as soon as I got inside, but my phone immediately chirped back an auto-reply telling me all the classes were filled. 
When Unc came in, clutching the hat, I wiped the frown off my face and asked, “How'd it go?” 
He made a humorless snort, and said “Well, it seemed like they might take the financial hardship claim seriously until her attourney brought up the fact that I'm selling the ranch. He'd printed off a bunch of those classifieds we took out. The judge said he'd consider the request again in six months.” 
“That's good news,” I said, trying to cheer him up. “All we have to do is not make the sale, then I'm sure he'll grant us an exemption and we can put it all behind us.” 
“Maybe,” he said, shaking his head. “But that's not the point. Y--we owe her,” he said, the frustration in his voice apparent. He should have said, almost did say: You owe her. 
I couldn't say anything to that, so I just said, “I'm going for a ride.”

Josey fought against the cuffs, his wrists aching, but the three coppers held him, two by
the arms and one by the back of his dingy overalls.
"Do I look like Dutch royalty to you?" He hurled the words like spittle and then hocked and
spat phlegm on the jailhouse floor. It wasn't a lie exactly. It was true, he looked more like he'd
just come off a chain gang than a royal frigate. Moreover his deep, woody irises and blackolive
skin bespoke anything but royal linaeage.
"Who you think you're foolin?"
"I'm from Trinidad," shouted Josey, "just look at me. I'm no Dutchman!"
"Could be black Dutch," said a fourth cop, calmly filling out paperwork on a clipboard,
"anyway it ain't none of my business, all's I know is I got orders to arrest one Josiah Davis
Coelho. And, according to your papers, that's you."
"You got the wrong guy!" coughed Josey. "Just look at my papers, I'm no Dutchman.
Don't you see, whoever you're looking for--they're--they're just using my name. Anybody could
have gotten hold of the manifest and--"
"Shut yer trap, prisoner," said the beefiest of the four cops, a young man of an officer who
looked almost as tough as Josey himself.
"He ain't Dutch."
The voice came from behind, but Josey couldn't see who was speaking. He tried to
stand, but the cops were putting the weight of three men on him, forcing his knees to grind
concrete.
"Could be black Dutch," said one of the coppers.
"Ain't no such thing," came the voice again.
"And what do you know?" The younger cop let go and spun around to face the
newcomer. "Oh," he gasped, "Sargeant van Niedermeijer. I didn't realize--"
Josey tried to shake free of the two remaining cops, only to be wrestled to the floor, face
in the dust.
"You trying to say I don't know what a fuckin Dutch looks like? Is your name Sargeant van
Niedermeijer?"
"No," mumbled the young officer, looking down as he abruptly doffed his hat.
"Speak up rookie, I'm talking to you."
"No, sir! Um... I mean... Sorry, I meant, 'No sir, Sargeant.'"
"Alright then. Let the negro go," said van Niedermeijer.
"I'm Indian," said Josey.
"What?"
"I'm no negro, I'm East Indian," repeated Josey.
"Shut your trap and count your blessings, because you're off the hook for now. Now get
out of my sight." Sargeant van Niedermeijer took the clipboard and shuffled around a corner as
the other coppers led Josey, still cuffed, to the station counter and waited in line behind a couple
of prostitutes and a man with the dull red eyes of an addict. The young officer held his hat in his
hand and all of them waited silently while paperwork shuffled across the desk. Josey glanced
around expectantly at the coppers' stony faces.
Finally, "I thought you were going to let me go," said Josey.
"We'll get you your stuff and have you on your way just as soon as possible," replied the
young officer in a polite but unapologetic tone.
More than half an hour later, they reached the counter and the haggered old cop behind
it, who said, "You sure this ain't the guy? He matches the description posted in the head."

"Yeah," said the young officer, "we gotta let the negro go. Straight from van Niedermeijer."
"Alright," said the older cop as he pulled out the evidence box from under the counter,
"here's your belongings." He eyed Josey suspiciously but said nothing more.
One of the cops asked the other behind the counter to fetch the suspect description for
them to read, then he unshackled Josey's wrists and said, "You're free to go, Mr. Coelho. Grab
your stuff and get going."
In the beat-up wooden box were belongings that had been pulled out of Josey's pockets
by his arresting officers--a pouch of tobacco, rolling papers, and a mother-of-pearl pen knife
attached to a small ring of keys. He noticed two things immediately: First, his six silver dollars
and change were gone. This was no surprise, of course. Josey had been arrested before, and
lifting a suspect's cash and coin was the closest he had yet seen to "standard procedure".
What was surprising to Josey, however, was the second thing he noticed: There were
several objects here that had definitely not been in his pockets when he'd gotten jumped by the
coppers on his way home from the docks--an enormous red stone set in a heavy pewter thumb
ring, two other little pewter objects that looked like they might be lockets of some sort, and a city
map. Josey thought it looked like a map of Brooklyn, though he didn't recognize anything
specifically, and there were no labels on the streets.
Josey gathered the small objects into his pockets and paused, momentarily at a loss as
to where he could keep the large, rolled map. Seeing the old cop return to the desk inspecting a
sheet of paper with a puzzled look on his face, saying "You sure that ain't him?" Josey stuffed
the map down his undershirt and quickly fled. One of the other officers said "Hey there, just you
wait a minute." Josey pretended not to hear and walked as calmly as he could down the short
hall to the station's entryway. "Get back here!" His heart was racing, but he made it to the front
steps just as shouts of "Get him!" and a roar of footfalls raised behind him.
Josey darted into the crowded Manhattan street, clutching the strange map in his shirt as
he dodged between businessmen and society ladies. He was on the run once more.

Old Man Treller snorted when Josey walked in, barely lifting his eyes from the purchases

inexplicably greasy. He didn't wait for a reply before going on, "You logged all these purchases
yesterday, didn't you Josey? You bought way too many; our lot ain't big enought to house all
these jalopies."
"Morning to you too, bossman," said Josey. "What's a 'jalopy'?" All his experience with oil
rigging had prepared him well for life as an auto mechanic, and in the months since he left New
York, he'd tried to erase all traces of his accent--by now his pronunciation sounded just like the
locals. Still, Midwestern auto jargon wasn't the same as Trini oil jargon.
"Cars, Josey, cars."
"Ah. Well, I just wanted to pull some parts off those. I'll have them out of your way in no
time, boss. I've been wanting to build a racer and that Pierce Arrow is the best for the job," said
Josey. "I was hoping I could arrange a deal to buy them off you."
Treller tossed down the purchase list and made a stymieing face. "Deal? Whaddaya think
w'ere running some kinda island bazaar here? You got some kind of nerve, buddy. Remember
who's working for who here. And what do you got to deal with anyway?"
"Well, I did get those jalopies for next to nothing," said Josey Davis Coelho.
"Have you actually taken a look at that Pierce? I don't know why you think that'd be a
good racer. The thing's useless." said Treller.

"The body is, but the engine is a real piece of work. 1918 Pierce Arrow 66. That's a
monster and I was thinking if I souped it up--"
"Josey," interrupted Treller,"get your priorities straight. I need shit I can sell. That's what
pays your wages."
"But the engine was the fastest thing ever made for production. That's 848 cubic inches
of power. "All I need to do is get it running pull some parts from those other cars, and I'll have
twice the machine I used for my runs back east," said Josey.
"Now you think you're gonna do some more moonshine runs? Didn't you tell me you had
enough?"
"Yeah, I definitely have had enough of the bootleg business. Unfortunately, my landlady
isn't done collecting my rent, and the market's running out of vendors who'll give me a tab. And
don't forget I owe you pelnty too," said Josey. "You'd take the biggest cut, Mr. Treller. But, if you
think the business is getting too dangerous, I'll just have to make ends meet some other way."
"No, no, no. I didn't say that. I'd be thilled if you did something to bring any kind of profits
into the shop. Anyway, if you think I would forget what you owe me, you're out of your head."
Treller chuckled and rubbed his scruffy double chin. "I'll take a twenty percent cut," he said, "and
that's on top of what you already owe me."
"Twenty percent? How about ten? If I get kicked out of my apartment, I'll be too busy
living out of the car to use it for any moonshining."
"I ain't going lower than fifteen on the first run," insisted Treller.
"Alright, fifteen, plus what I owe you. But I get to keep the car, and then it's ten percent
after the first run." If there's one thing Josey learned from his dad, it's how to bargain. These
Americans didn't know what hit them most of the time, but Treller was pretty sure footed himself.
"It's a deal."
"Alright," said Josey, and they shook on it. "I'll set up a trip to Shinetown straightaway."
"Nah," said Treller, still grasping Josey's hand. "I was thinking you could do me a favor
since I'm giving you such a good deal. See, I got a source up in Newark."
"Down in Newark," corrected Josey.
"Yeah, whatever. My cousiln lives up there and he could use the business. That
Appalachian stuff is competition for him. Anyway, I could use some drinking stock for myself--I'd
pay you, of course--but the Shinetown sources always tasted like rotten eggs to me," said
Treller.
"Hmm. Your cousin in Newark, this guy is a big time moonshiner, then? Shiners down in
Shinetown, are cheap and that means lots of profit for us," said Josey.
"I know what that means, but if you want my charity to build your car, and if you want that
engine you bought with my money, you're making a trip to Newark. Where you go after that ain't
my business. Just so long as I get my fair share," said Treller.
"Alright, good deal," said Josey as he yanked his hand back from Treller's grip. "Good
enough, anyway."
Treller went back to whatever he'd been doing and Josey ran his hand giddily over the
car's rust welts and rough primer, ignoring the spurs that caught on his callused hands."You and
me baby," he said, "You and me."
Josey put in a light day of work for the shop, fixing and tuning up the new purchases
before washing them, parking them on the street, and soaping prices on the windows. He
ignored the old Pierce Arrow except occasionally to run a finger along the fender when he
walked into the back for a grease can or pliers.
At 5:00, with the sun low in the sky, Josey clocked out and went upstairs to his apartment
for a can of beans and a warm ginger ale. He looked around his spatan room for a container to
dump the junk and scraps from his car. All he had was the weathered wooden box wich doubled
as a stool and a stepladder, and sometimes in the summer as a doorstop for the fire escape. He
was surprised by the sound of something knocking around in the box when he picked it up, and
opening it, he remembered that's where he'd tossed the mysterious map and ring. He had come
to Columbus because of the map, but having found nothing special besides a good place to lay
low, the mystery of the map had faded from his mind. Now, he decided it would be a good
accessory for the car, so he tucked it under his arm and tucked the ring under the pillow on his
bed and went back downstairs to the shop and started cleaning out the inside of the car. Josey

worked late into the night. He gave himself three nights to get it running smooth. He could have
done it more quickly, but he wanted to take his time and do it right.
He would work on the interior tonight, oiling the leather panels and patching the holes in
the floors. Tomorrow he'd work on the engine, and after that all he had to do was the sagging
suspension. The body work would be kept to a minimum. If the cops thought it was a scrap job,
they wouldn't be ready for a chase.
Since the inside would be his home away from home, Josey took care to make it
comfortable. He lifted some nice velvet seats from the shell of the Studibaker President that sat
in the back of the lot for months until it had been canibalised down to bare skeleton. After he

The floorboards were covered in junk, a bent screwdriver, reciepts written in court
cursive, and beer cans that had been opened with what looked to be nail holes, or maybe the
holes were from the screwdriver.
Josey went to the map into the cubby hole on the passenger side. He paused to take
another look. The map's strangeness struck him again. On the one side, it was a map of
Columbus, Ohio--on the other side, was what appeared to be another map of Columbus, but a

Columbus side showed a lopsided city on the elbow of the Scioto river, a blocky grid cut by
occasional diagonals and curves and divided into quadrants by High Street and Broad Street--
streets with which he'd since become very familiar. The other side was a beautiful pinwheel of
avenues branching off a main hub. It was lovely and intricate and symetrical and it was nestled

Josey shook his head again in wonderment, still unable to make sense of it, and tossed it

The work went well, despite the caked dirt and grease on the underside of the engine.
