TITLE: The Damps
(c) 2006 By Nathan McKnight




Mr. Eberts drove through the night to make sure he arrived in Straitsville right at sun up. He figured he'd need most of a day's work to get the deal done, and he wanted to be out of there come nightfall. Already, he looked over his shoulder at every knock of the engine and flutter of the heart.  
*   *   *
"She's been running from that fire her whole goddamn life," said Mr. Eberts, "What makes you think she's going to stop running now?"
"Please, Bill," said Mr. Ambrose. "It would mean an awful lot. That woman practically raised me." 
Mr. Eberts finished the last crumbs of his lemon chiffon.
"Okay," he said, "but if I talk to Lizzie Green, you have to buy every last drop of Hock-Hocking I've got left."
"Hang on a sec," injected J.M., leaning over from the little window booth, "You ain't really going up to Lizzie Green's? That place ain't right, I tell ya. You're like as not to get snuffed out by mine gasses. And all that sulphur in the air--I'm telling ya--it'll eat yer eyes right outta yer head."
"This whole dang town smells like sulphur," said Mr. Eberts, "Gives me the creeps. It's why I left."
Eberts pushed his plate away.
"Don't have much choice," said Eberts. "If I don't sell this beer--and quick--I'm out of a job."
"The way I hear it, you're out of luck any case," said J.M., waving his fried egg sandwich.
"Maybe," said Eberts, "but if I unload my last few cases, I'll get my severance, and a crack at a position in the new company."
"New company?"
"The brewery's thinking of switching to soda pop come the new year."
That brought a guffaw that blew the whipped cream off J.M.'s milkshake.
"Nobody's gonna be drinkin soda pop, Mr. Eberts. If they really take away whiskey, folks around here'll just switch to mine rum."
"It's a done deal," said Eberts, turning back to Mr. Ambrose, "Prohibition is coming. So, what about us? Do we have a deal?" 
He stuck out his hand, Ambrose yanked it toward him, Eberts yanked it back, they shook high, shook low, and ended in an Indian-style "How!"
Just like old times.
"One last thing," said Mr. Eberts. 
He scribbled out a note on the back of his napkin. 
"Could I ask you to send a telegram to Hocking Brewery?" he said.
Ambrose took the napkin and read it aloud: "SALE CONFIRMED SEND THREE TRUCKS PAREN. SEVEN-FIFTY CASES CLOSE PAREN. STRAITSVILLE. A-S-A-P."
*   *   *
He could feel the breath of the ghost horses on the back window of his car as he sped up the road to Dutch Ridge. They had haunted him all his life, but the ghost hooves pounded on his trail as he fishtailed around a gravelly corner. 
He shook his head, took one hand at a time off the wheel to shake out the knucklewhite. He never should have returned to New Straitsville. 
A veil of smoke encompassed the car, and Eberts cursed. The mine fire had been burning since '94. He'd only been eleven at the time, but he way he remembered it, the Sun had died the day the striking workers started the fire. Not long afterwards, Grampa Lisander had died fighting for the town that vilified him. Family enmity burned long in these parts.

Author's Intro to The Gilgamesh Golem

The following story, "The Gilgamesh Golem", was originally published in "the tloating liars' club", a slick DIY fiction magazine with a circulation of about 300, which ran for three issues, plus one finished but unpublished issue between late 2002 and mid-2003. The magazine was published by Nathan McKnight, along with Joe Bellomy (his father and sometimes coauthor), Shannon Rampe (a writer working in Arlington, VA) and Ben Crites (a fantastic writer we've kind of lost contact with over the years, apart from a couple of serendipitous bumpings-into). The four wrote almost all of the stories, with the exception of a couple of pieces written by close friends Jade Seven and Lauren Rampe. McKnight took the lead in pushing the writers' group to come together to showcase their talent. Bellomy did almost all of the art (with the exception of one story illustrated by Jade Seven--"Save the Kildans", an extremely experimental science fiction piece by McKnight). Bellomy's color cover art is raw and beautiful, rough but detailed, and his black and white interior spot illos range from haunting to playful. 

McKnight started this story in the wake of 9/11. See if you can spot the political allusions in the text. Hint: If the religous subject matter doesn't say it all, look closely at the names, remembering McKnight's often subtle--but often not--wordplay. 


TITLE: The Gilgamesh Golem
(c) 2003 by Nathan McKnight



 This may be the last story ever written. I write it to God, who would leave me alone on this Earth where all the nations have worn down to plains. The minerals that compose me come from the beginning of the world, shaped by wind and time. But the spirit that inhabits this clay form is human, shaped by other humans. I've waited the lifetimes of races to be discovered by some visitor or some god, and perhaps my hope will yet be borne out in the short time I have left. But, if the end-times sun undoes the magic that made me or bakes my limbs into useless branches, you should know that it is the same kilny sun whose light I count on to envitrify my words into the soft clay before the salt-laden tides of the last sea smother them out.

The story begins in Jewish Harlem, before the southern blacks replaced the Jews, before the Hispanic migrants replaced the blacks, before the Arab refugees replaced the migrants, and before the Israilis replaced them…

* * *

Paul's mother was displeased in the extreme when she found out that her money was coming from boxing. She had stopped taking the blood money, as she called it, when word got around the neighborhood that Paul "The Maul" Stein had ended a fight by clocking one of the Italian boys and blinding him in one eye. Consequently, Paul and his fiancée had a modest savings.

They had planned to get married in grand fashion, possibly even in their own semi-luxurious apartment whose neo-Egyptian façade was shaded during the hottest Scene of the afternoon by the shadow of the new Empire State building, where Holly worked as an assistant executive secretary. It was the nature of their respective professions that they spent most of the day apart. Their only contact was at dinnertime, after Holly had spent a long day in the office without a break and Paul was readying himself for the evening's fight. Sometimes, the famished couple would go back to Harlem where Yiddish and Italian and Irish voices filled the air with the restless spirits of the old countries, voices that complimented Mother Stein's cooking like the spices of the east. Holly would impress them with anecdotes of rich foreigners who always seemed to make extraordinary demands of the secretaries or, on lucky days, to bestow upon them ludicrously large tips in exchange for everyday kindness.

It was on one such occasion that Paul first heard the name Israel ben Muhammad. Holly normally paid scant attention to changes of leadership in the company, but the buy-out by an Arabian oil baron precipitated an especially large shake-up among the employees. The stars portend opportunity, Mrs. Stein had told her son knowingly. Indeed, Holly ended up filling her own supervisor's newly vacant position as lead executive secretary, handling the appointment books of ben Muhammad himself. Paul learned of her new boss's real estate aspirations on the same day that the change in management for the East Central apartment buildings took effect. Notices were first posted to inform the residents on that very day. They were on all the walls and in all the mailboxes. They were given by hand to every occupant, sometimes more than once. The postings shrouded the fine sheeny wallpaper with a quiltwork of mottled parchment. In order to keep the "criminal element" at bay—some anti-Arab graffitoism had taken place in the otherwise immaculate children's daytime care facility—all residents were asked to carry punch cards. In addition, for reasons that were poorly explained, rent would be upped for certain occupants. Paul and Holly would have to pay more than triple the normal due.

Scene 1. HELLFIRE

"Hellfire!"
      That's what Pa had called it. I dropped the jar, shaking my finger in the air. It didn't hurt really; just a little sting. But it startled me enough to make me jump. I looked down. It wasn't broken, but I was dumbfounded for a second.

I?d nearly broken it, but this time when the snap! and the light pricked my finger, I didn't drop it. I was giddy. If Pa hadn't told me the story about finding the hellfire jar, I wouldn't know what it was, let alone what to do with it. 
      But this...well, this had potential. 
* * *
      "Hellfire!" Pa coughed, "That's what Gramps called it," Pa had said when I was a kid. "Him and Uncle Topher went out beagling like usual, and they took me and Pauli along with. That was before we started horsing. Every week, they?d send out the terriers to sniff out fox, with the beagles following them up, and me and Pauli on the little horses and Gramps and Topher on a double."

You ain't never seen a foxhunt, so you won't know what that's like--I should send you over to the Johnses to learn--"
      I remember having rolled my eyes. Father was always trying to get me into the things he loved as a child. Foxing, birding... But beagling was for farmers. 
      "No way, Pops," I had said, "I?m a city boy. I was made for horsing." 
      Father had laughed and I sat forward on the edge of my seat.
      "True that, true that," said father. "Well, anyway, them terriers, they all went down a hole. All down the same hole. That's how we knew something strange was going on. A foxhole's a little thing, son. I only got to go a couple times before we stopped the hunts, but even so, I knew enough foxholes to recognize you couldn't fit twelve of any kind of hound down one burrow. Turns out, it wasn't no burrow."  
      "What was it?" I asked.
      "If I tell you," he said, "you have to keep it secret."

      After school, the day after I found the jar, Brian caught up to me at the postal coop when I was rolling my transcripts. I had applied for every damn college in riding distance, but hadn't heard back from a single one of them. I was starting to get desperate.

      I slid my transcripts into a tube and turned to the closest roadrunner. "Thirty-five cent," it squawked. Must?ve been a slow learner.
	I handed over thirty-seven cents and it snatched the tube from my hands before disappearing into the coop.

	"That's because you applied for a bunch of out-of-state schools, didn't you?" said Brian.
	"Uh--yeah," I lied.
	"So, don't worry about it. Pigeons only fly so fast." 
	"Easy for you to say, you got into MID." 
      The Massachusetts Institute of Domestication was the top school in the country for breed/train majors. 
      "Get your mind off it," he said, "Me and Courtney are going to head out to the Rock tonight. Want to come?"
      "Naw, I?d be the fifth leg."
      "Courtney's friends with Ella, you know."
      "Ella?" I could feel my face warm. "Can you get her to come out with us?"
      "I can ask." 
      "Isn't she going out with...Lester McCoy?" I practically growled his name.
